summary:
La Araucanía is a region of Chile with no regional variant of the national rules, so a trans visitor's legal position there is set by Chilean statute, courts and administrative practice.

Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must go to the family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute does not provide for those under 14, although it recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Recorded anti-trans and homophobic violence in La Araucanía is rising faster than anywhere else in Chile. Movilh's XXIV annual human-rights report, published in March 2026 on 2025 data, ranked the region first in year-on-year growth in recorded cases, up 150%, and put La Araucanía at 1.96% of the national case total. The same report recorded a national figure of 3,620 documented cases for 2025, 27.1% above 2024, with that single year accounting for 23% of all cases across the 24-year series.

Lethal and near-lethal transphobic violence is documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a hotel in Santiago, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Care access has both protection and pressure on it. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
La Araucanía's 150% year-on-year rise comes off a small base: the region accounted for 1.96% of the national case total in 2025. Percentage growth of that magnitude therefore reflects a low starting figure as well as a genuine deterioration, and it is the direction of travel rather than the regional share that stands out.

The regional trend runs against a national pattern that is itself worsening. Movilh's 2025 national total of 3,620 documented cases exceeded 2024 by 27.1%, and 2025 alone represents 23% of everything recorded in the organisation's 24-year series. Higher recorded counts reflect both more incidents and increased willingness to report, which the source does not separate.

Legal protection and political hostility coexist in the current Chilean framework. Hate-motivated offences are aggravated under the Zamudio Law and the Constitutional Court has twice struck down statutory limits on trans minors' rights, while the Chamber of Deputies has endorsed a package of restrictive recommendations and Congress has removed funding from one support programme.

Chile's asylum provisions place it among the jurisdictions that name gender identity expressly in removal protections, which is relevant to anyone arriving from a country where transition or public identification carries criminal risk.

Ministry of Health-run support in medical centres continues after Congress removed funding for the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program in the 2026 Budget Law. The Crece con Orgullo programme has served children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 since 2023.

outOfScopeNotes:
The 150% regional increase is reported only as a percentage and a 1.96% share of the national total; absolute case numbers for La Araucanía in 2024 and 2025 are not stated in the inventory, so the size of the underlying problem cannot be verified from these sources.

Whether the recorded rise in La Araucanía reflects specific local actors, incidents or reporting drives is not addressed in the sources, and no breakdown by incident type, location within the region, or police response is available here.

The inventory does not indicate whether regional health services in La Araucanía offer adolescent gender care, how Circular 7 of June 2024 has been applied locally, or whether Crece con Orgullo operates in the region; these remain unsourced.

No information is available on whether the Gendarmería de Chile protocol has been implemented at detention facilities within La Araucanía, or on any regional policing or hate-crime unit specific to the region.

The outcome of the CEI 57 recommendations after 15 May 2025, and whether any of the four measures proposed were enacted, is not covered by the sources. The same is true of the effect of the defunded Ministry of Social Development programme on residents who previously used it.

No regional-level anti-discrimination body, equality council or dedicated support facility for trans visitors in La Araucanía appears anywhere in the inventory, and the absence of such a body here is not established either way.
